snapshot.statement:
A data engineering team runs a nightly pipeline that reads Delta tables, applies PySpark transformations, and writes a gold table. The pipeline is executed by a Lakeflow Job and must use dedicated compute that starts when the job starts and is terminated automatically when the job finishes. Analysts must not be able to attach to this compute for interactive sessions.

Which compute option should the team use for this workload?
options: An all-purpose cluster that stays running so analysts can attach to it between job runs
A job cluster scoped to the Lakeflow Job, created and terminated by the job itself
A serverless SQL warehouse configured for the notebook tasks in the job
A high-concurrency cluster shared with other teams that run ad hoc queries
snapshot.referenceTitle: Compute for Lakeflow Jobs — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A company currently exports data from its operational systems to Parquet files in cloud object storage. Analysts want to run ad hoc SQL queries over that data, and data scientists want to train models on the exact same tables. Both teams need ACID guarantees, reliable schema, and a single source of truth — without maintaining two separate copies of the data in a warehouse and a data lake.

Which approach directly addresses these requirements on the Databricks Data Intelligence Platform?
options: Keep two copies of the data: load it into a classic data warehouse for the analysts and keep the raw files in the lake for the data scientists
Adopt the lakehouse approach: use the Delta Lake open table format on cloud object storage, with Unity Catalog governing access for all teams
Store everything as ephemeral in-memory DataFrames and recompute them from source whenever either team needs the data
Convert all data to unstructured JSON files so both teams can parse them with their own custom readers
snapshot.referenceTitle: Introduction to the Databricks Data Intelligence Platform

snapshot.statement:
A healthcare company is migrating its analytics to the Databricks Data Intelligence Platform. Its security officers need one central place to define who can access which tables across all workspaces, to track lineage, and to audit query activity for compliance reporting. They do not want to manage access rules separately in each cloud storage account.

Which platform component is the foundation for these requirements?
options: Unity Catalog, the lakehouse's unified governance layer, with centralized permissions, lineage, and auditing
Delta Lake, which enforces access rules inside the table format through the ACID transaction log it maintains on every write
Serverless SQL warehouses, which automatically apply row-level filters to every query they execute
Lakeflow Jobs, which can grant and revoke privileges each time a scheduled task runs
snapshot.referenceTitle: Introduction to the Databricks Data Intelligence Platform

snapshot.statement:
A two-person data engineering team schedules a nightly Lakeflow Job that runs a PySpark notebook to refresh reporting tables. The team has no cluster administration expertise and wants to avoid selecting instance types, worker counts, or runtime versions. They also want the job's compute to become available quickly, with no infrastructure for them to deploy or configure.

Which compute option best fits these requirements?
options: Serverless compute for jobs, which Databricks provisions, scales, and manages automatically
A classic job cluster with manually selected worker instance types and autoscaling bounds
A shared all-purpose cluster that remains running so the job can attach to it at night
A classic job cluster that the team resizes each evening based on the previous run
snapshot.referenceTitle: Compute for Lakeflow Jobs — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A BI team connects Tableau and Power BI to the Databricks workspace over JDBC/ODBC and spends the day running ad hoc SQL queries and dashboards against gold Delta tables. Analysts do not want to size or tune Spark clusters; they need compute that is optimized for SQL analytics and BI workloads and that starts and scales on demand with query traffic.

Which compute service should the team use?
options: A classic all-purpose Spark cluster with Photon enabled, shared by all analysts
A SQL warehouse, the compute optimized for SQL queries, analytics, and business intelligence workloads
A classic job cluster scoped to a nightly Lakeflow Job, which the BI tools would have to connect to during the day while it stays running
Serverless compute for jobs, because the BI tools schedule their queries as job tasks
snapshot.referenceTitle: Compute — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A data engineering team is migrating a legacy Spark application into a Lakeflow Job. One task in the job must run a compiled JAR that the team maintains. The team would prefer to run the entire job on serverless compute for jobs to avoid managing clusters.

Which statement is correct?
options: The JAR task can run on serverless compute for jobs once the JAR is uploaded as a dependent library
The JAR task must run on a serverless SQL warehouse, because SQL warehouses execute compiled artifacts
JAR tasks are not supported on serverless compute for jobs — that task needs classic jobs compute
Serverless compute for jobs supports every task type; the team only needs to pick a Databricks Runtime version
snapshot.referenceTitle: Compute for Lakeflow Jobs — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A machine learning team works interactively in notebooks, training models on GPU-enabled instances with Databricks Runtime for Machine Learning and several custom environment libraries. To reduce administration, they ask whether this workload can move to serverless compute.

What should the data engineer answer?
options: Yes — serverless compute automatically attaches GPU instances when it detects ML libraries
Yes — serverless compute supports every Databricks Runtime version, including ML runtimes
No — interactive GPU training must be submitted as separate Lakeflow Jobs that each create a job cluster
No — ML Runtime on GPU is not supported on serverless compute; use a classic compute resource
snapshot.referenceTitle: Classic compute configuration best practices — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A retail company wants its data quality notebook to run automatically every night at 02:00, to retry the task if it fails, and to email the on-call engineer whenever a run fails. The notebook already exists in the workspace.

Which platform capability should the company use?
options: Databricks Git Folders (formerly Repos), which run notebooks on a schedule from a Git branch
Unity Catalog, which governs data access and can also schedule notebook refreshes
Delta Lake time travel, which can rewind and replay a notebook's previous outputs
Lakeflow Jobs, which schedule the notebook with retries and failure notifications
snapshot.referenceTitle: Lakeflow Jobs — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A streaming media company is designing its ingestion layer on the Databricks Data Intelligence Platform. It has three sources:

- A legacy billing system that delivers a complete extract of all open invoices every Sunday night
- A partner that drops small CSV files into an Amazon S3 bucket several times per hour
- A website that emits click events continuously to a message bus

Which mapping of ingestion pattern to source is correct?
options: Billing extract: streaming ingestion; partner CSVs: reload the entire bucket on every run; click events: weekly scheduled batch
All three sources: nightly batch with full reprocessing, because batch processing keeps track of what has already been processed
Billing extract: batch load; partner CSVs: incremental loading of only the newly arrived files; click events: streaming ingestion
Billing extract: incremental load keyed by invoice ID; partner CSVs: stateful streaming deduplication; click events: hourly batch of the previous hour
snapshot.referenceTitle: Batch vs. streaming data processing — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A product manager e-mails the data engineering team a weekly CSV export that lives on her laptop. The team needs its contents in a Unity Catalog-governed Delta table and plans to run this statement once the file is available on a storage path:

```sql
COPY INTO main.ops.weekly_orders
FROM '/Volumes/main/ingest/uploads/'
FILEFORMAT = CSV;
```

Which approach correctly makes the laptop file available to this statement?
options: Point the FROM clause at the file path on the product manager's laptop, such as 'C:/exports/orders.csv', because COPY INTO can read any path the analyst can open
Upload the file into a Unity Catalog volume (for example, with the Catalog Explorer upload option) so it lands on a UC-governed cloud storage path that COPY INTO can read
Place the file in the workspace DBFS root with dbutils.fs.put, because DBFS paths are automatically governed by Unity Catalog
Attach the CSV to a notebook cell and run spark.read.csv on the uploaded artifact, since notebook attachments behave like Unity Catalog tables
snapshot.referenceTitle: Get started using COPY INTO — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A data engineer schedules this statement as the single task of a nightly Lakeflow Job. The source folder accumulates Parquet files throughout the day:

```sql
COPY INTO main.ops.bookings_raw
FROM 'abfss://landing@storacct.dfs.core.windows.net/bookings/'
FILEFORMAT = PARQUET;
```

What happens on a night when no new files have arrived since the last successful run?
options: The statement completes successfully and loads zero rows, because files that were already loaded by previous runs are skipped
The statement fails with a duplicate-file error, because COPY INTO re-inserts every file in the folder on every run
The statement reloads all files, and the team must schedule a MERGE job afterwards to remove the duplicates
The statement blocks until new files arrive, because COPY INTO behaves like a streaming source waiting for data
snapshot.referenceTitle: Get started using COPY INTO — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A team must load JSON booking updates from a Unity Catalog volume with COPY INTO. The producer occasionally adds new fields, so the files do not all share the same schema, and the team wants new fields to appear in the target table automatically instead of causing failures. The target table has not been created yet.

Which approach meets these requirements?
options: Create the table with an explicit schema listing every column seen so far, so that COPY INTO fails fast whenever a file carries an unexpected field
Create an empty table without declaring columns and set the table property 'delta.columnMapping.mode' = 'name' so unmatched JSON fields map automatically
Read each day's files with spark.read.json, union them with the existing table, and overwrite the table nightly, because COPY INTO cannot handle differing schemas
Create an empty table without declaring columns, then run COPY INTO with 'mergeSchema' = 'true' in FORMAT_OPTIONS and COPY_OPTIONS
snapshot.referenceTitle: Get started using COPY INTO — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A newly hired data engineer runs the following statement in a workspace where Unity Catalog manages all data access:

```sql
COPY INTO main.ops.shipments
FROM 'abfss://raw@companylake.dfs.core.windows.net/shipments/'
FILEFORMAT = PARQUET;
```

The target table exists, but the statement fails with a path access error. What must be configured before COPY INTO can read this location?
options: A DBFS mount point for the storage account, because COPY INTO can only read paths that are mounted under /mnt
A Unity Catalog storage credential and an external location for the path, with READ FILES granted
The storage account key embedded directly in the FROM clause, so COPY INTO authenticates on each run
An ingestion gateway deployed next to the storage account's private endpoint
snapshot.referenceTitle: Get started using COPY INTO — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A team copies this snippet from an old tutorial to ingest JSON files that keep arriving in a Unity Catalog volume:

```python
df = (spark.read
  .format("cloudFiles")
  .option("cloudFiles.format", "json")
  .load("/Volumes/main/ingest/events/"))
```

The job runs on a schedule, but each run never picks up files that arrived after the very first execution, and no schema inference is configured.

Which change turns this into a working Auto Loader stream with schema inference and evolution?
options: Switch the reader to spark.readStream.format("cloudFiles") and keep everything else unchanged, because schema inference needs no additional options
Keep spark.read and add .option("cloudFiles.schemaLocation", ...) to the reader, since the batch reader supports Auto Loader options too
Use spark.readStream.format("cloudFiles") with cloudFiles.format and a durable cloudFiles.schemaLocation for schema inference and evolution
Replace format("cloudFiles") with format("streamingFiles") and set checkpointLocation on the reader, because schemaLocation only applies to Delta targets
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Auto Loader? — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
An Auto Loader stream that feeds a Unity Catalog-governed Delta table failed in the middle of the night after processing part of the incoming file batch. In the morning, the on-call engineer restarts the stream from the same notebook, pointing at the same input directory, checkpoint location, and target table.

What does Auto Loader guarantee after the restart?
options: It resumes where it left off: files already recorded in checkpoint state are not reprocessed, preserving exactly-once semantics
It starts over and re-ingests every file in the input directory, so the on-call engineer must schedule a deduplication job after every recovery
It skips the partially processed files and leaves a gap that must be backfilled manually before the next run
It truncates the target Delta table and reloads all files so the table returns to a consistent state
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Auto Loader? — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
To reduce storage costs, a cloud administrator applies a 30-day lifecycle expiration rule to every prefix under the S3 bucket that hosts an Auto Loader stream's checkpoint directory. The stream has run daily for two months against the same input directory.

What is the impact, and what should the team have done instead?
options: No impact: the checkpoint is rebuilt automatically from the target table's Delta transaction log on the next run
Auto Loader silently switches to file notification mode and re-lists the entire input directory tree on every micro-batch, because its checkpoint state has gone missing
Only files from the last 30 days are reprocessed, because Delta time travel caps recovery at 30 days
The stream state is corrupted and it must restart from scratch, likely reprocessing files; checkpoints belong in durable storage outside lifecycle rules
snapshot.referenceTitle: Auto Loader best practices — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
An Auto Loader stream reads files that land in Amazon S3 at a rate that has grown to hundreds of thousands of files per hour spread over a deep directory tree. The stream uses directory listing mode with a continuous trigger, and monthly cloud bills show ever-increasing S3 LIST request charges. The team can obtain the elevated cloud permissions required for notification setup.

Which change best addresses the cost and scalability problem?
options: Keep directory listing mode and raise cloudFiles.fetchParallelism so that the directory tree is listed more quickly
Switch to file notification mode: file events go to a queue that the stream consumes, scaling far beyond listing
Require producers to write into a single flat directory so that each run needs only one LIST call
Replace Auto Loader with a scheduled COPY INTO statement, because COPY INTO lists the directory more cheaply than Auto Loader
snapshot.referenceTitle: Auto Loader file notification mode — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A team runs Auto Loader against Amazon S3 in classic file notification mode: they set cloudFiles.useNotifications to true and grant Auto Loader the permissions it needs to create cloud resources in the bucket.

Which resources does Auto Loader create so that newly uploaded files are announced to the stream?
options: An AWS Lambda function that watches the bucket and writes new object keys to a DynamoDB table that Auto Loader polls
An Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream that receives ObjectCreated events and feeds them into an SQS queue
An Amazon SNS topic subscribed to the bucket's object-created notifications, with an Amazon SQS queue that Auto Loader consumes
An Azure Event Grid subscription and an Azure Queue Storage queue, which Databricks uses as its cross-cloud default
snapshot.referenceTitle: Auto Loader file notification mode — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A bank's security policy forbids creating event notification services or queues in its cloud storage accounts. The data team still wants Auto Loader to ingest new files from a modest source directory that receives a few dozen files per day, with minimal setup.

Which file discovery mode should the team use, and why?
options: File notification mode with file events, because managed file events require no cloud permission grants at all
Classic file notification mode, because the team can create the queues themselves instead of letting Auto Loader do it
Plain batch reads with spark.read, because Auto Loader cannot run without notification services
Directory listing mode: the default, needing no cloud permissions beyond read access to the storage path
snapshot.referenceTitle: Auto Loader directory listing mode — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
Event files like the one below arrive continuously in a UC volume, and the team starts Auto Loader with schema inference (no explicit schema, cloudFiles.schemaLocation set):

```json
{"user_id": 1042, "event_ts": "2026-05-01T10:22:31Z", "amount": 49.9, "profile": {"tier": "gold", "region": "emea"}}
```

What schema does Auto Loader infer by default, and how can the team get typed columns such as numbers and timestamps?
options: All fields — including nested ones — are inferred as string; set cloudFiles.inferColumnTypes to true to infer types like long, double, and timestamp
user_id becomes long, amount becomes double, event_ts becomes timestamp, and profile becomes a struct, because Auto Loader always samples rows and picks the narrowest matching type
The profile object is rejected, because Auto Loader cannot infer nested structures from JSON files
Top-level fields are strings while nested fields keep their JSON types, so only profile.tier and profile.region are correctly typed
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Auto Loader? — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
An Auto Loader stream with an inferred schema has run for weeks using only the default schema evolution settings. This morning, the producer adds a new column loyalty_points to the JSON files.

What happens on the next micro-batch, and what does Databricks recommend operationally?
options: The new column is silently ignored forever; to add it, the team must edit the inferred schema files stored under the schema location
The stream keeps running with the old schema and quietly stores all loyalty_points values in the _rescued_data column, with no interruption at all
Auto Loader adds loyalty_points and the stream stops with UnknownFieldException; a restart resumes it with the new schema
The stream drops the offending files into a bad records path and keeps ingesting the remaining files with the old schema
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Auto Loader? — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A compliance feed must land in a table whose schema has to stay strictly stable — no automatic column additions. At the same time, the team cannot tolerate ingestion outages when the feed occasionally sends unexpected extra fields, and it wants those values preserved for later inspection.

Which cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode setting satisfies all three requirements?
options: addNewColumns — new fields are merged into the table schema and the stream resumes automatically
rescue — the schema never evolves, the stream never fails due to schema changes, and unexpected fields are recorded in the rescued data column
failOnNewColumns — the stream stops whenever a new field appears and stays down until someone updates the schema or removes the file
addNewColumnsWithTypeWidening — new fields are merged and compatible type changes are widened automatically
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Auto Loader? — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
An Auto Loader stream runs with an inferred schema. In today's batch, some records use a column name with different casing (OrderID instead of order_id), and one field's value does not match the type Auto Loader inferred for it.

Where does this non-conforming data end up?
options: The affected records are dropped silently; only a row-count discrepancy in the stream metrics hints that something was lost
The stream fails immediately, because case mismatches and type mismatches are fatal errors during schema inference
The mismatched values are redirected to the bad records path that Auto Loader configures by default for every stream
They land in the _rescued_data column Auto Loader adds automatically — non-conforming fields plus the source file path
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Auto Loader? — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
Auto Loader is ingesting the JSON events below with schema inference, so every field — nested ones included — is currently a string:

```json
{"event_ts": "2026-05-01T10:22:31Z", "amount": "49.90", "user_info": {"id": "1042", "dob": "1990-04-18"}}
```

The team wants event_ts read as TIMESTAMP, amount as DOUBLE, and user_info.dob as DATE, while all other fields keep being inferred automatically.

Which Auto Loader option does this?
options: cloudFiles.schemaHints, e.g. 'event_ts TIMESTAMP, amount DOUBLE, user_info.dob DATE' — pins known types, infers the rest
cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode set to addNewColumnsWithTypeWidening, which converts inferred strings into native types as data arrives
cloudFiles.inferColumnTypes together with a full .schema() declaration listing every column, including all nested fields
cloudFiles.rescuedDataColumn, which casts values rescued from type mismatches back into typed columns
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Auto Loader? — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A retailer wants to ingest files from cloud object storage into a Unity Catalog-governed table once per night. The pipeline should start on a schedule, process whatever files have arrived, and then stop, so the team pays only for a short run instead of compute that stays on around the clock.

Which design matches these requirements?
options: Start a stream with .trigger(processingTime='1 hour') and leave it running continuously, so each micro-batch picks up new files as they arrive
Use .trigger(availableNow=True): process all available data, then stop — scheduled via a time-based trigger in a Lakeflow Job
Run Trigger.Once inside a while loop in a single notebook so the stream never gets a chance to idle
Skip Auto Loader entirely and use a one-time spark.read.parquet, because Auto Loader cannot be used for scheduled batch-style loads
snapshot.referenceTitle: Auto Loader best practices — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A logistics company must ingest shipment telemetry from a supplier's bucket: roughly 5,000 new Parquet files per day arriving around the clock, volume growing about 20% per year, and the producer occasionally adds columns. The team wants low operational overhead with schema handled automatically. The SQL-first team lead proposes a scheduled COPY INTO statement that runs every 15 minutes.

What should the data engineering team recommend?
options: Accept COPY INTO — it scales to any file count and absorbs column changes as long as it runs frequently enough
Replace it with a nightly spark.read.parquet overwrite of the entire bucket, which avoids streaming checkpoints entirely
Use Auto Loader (e.g. a streaming table): incremental file tracking, very large scale, and schema inference with evolution
Query the supplier's operational database over JDBC instead, because file-based ingestion cannot keep up with around-the-clock arrivals
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Auto Loader? — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
Sales operations needs Salesforce data — accounts, opportunities, and their ongoing changes — replicated into Unity Catalog-governed Delta tables. The requirements are minimal operational overhead, no ingestion code for the team to maintain, change capture from the SaaS source, and full governance on the target tables.

Which approach should the data engineering team prioritize?
options: A nightly full CSV export from Salesforce into S3, loaded by a scheduled COPY INTO statement
A partner ELT tool deployed on the team's own compute that writes Parquet files to an external location
A custom Structured Streaming job against the Salesforce REST API, owned and maintained by the platform team, with the team patching and scaling its compute
The Lakeflow Connect managed Salesforce connector: serverless, Databricks-operated, landing in UC-governed streaming tables
snapshot.referenceTitle: Lakeflow Connect connector concepts — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
The team configures a Lakeflow Connect managed streaming connector for a Confluent Kafka topic that carries semi-structured JSON order events. Everything must live in Unity Catalog, and the team must not manage any compute for the ingestion.

Which set of components does Lakeflow Connect stand up, and how does the data flow?
options: A Unity Catalog connection for credentials, a serverless pipeline, and UC-governed streaming tables as destination
A job cluster that runs an Auto Loader notebook and writes Parquet files to an external location registered as a foreign catalog
An ingestion gateway virtual machine in the team's VPC plus staging storage that the team must size, patch, and monitor
A Lakeflow Job with a dbt task that materializes the topic into hourly materialized views
snapshot.referenceTitle: Lakeflow Connect connector concepts — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A notebook task extracts a 400-million-row table from a PostgreSQL data warehouse over JDBC. The current read runs on a single connection and takes hours:

```python
orders = (spark.read.format("jdbc")
  .option("url", jdbc_url)
  .option("dbtable", "sales.orders")
  .option("user", user)
  .option("password", pwd)
  .load())
```

How should the team parallelize the read, and what is the effect?
options: Set numPartitions=8 alone; Spark opens eight simultaneous queries against sales.orders without needing any column or bound options
Add partitionColumn (indexed, uniform), lowerBound, upperBound, and numPartitions; Spark runs concurrent range queries
Set fetchSize=100000 so each round trip pulls more rows through the existing single connection, which parallelizes the fetch
Set partitionColumn to the primary key and numPartitions=500 to maximize the number of simultaneous queries against the warehouse
snapshot.referenceTitle: Query databases using JDBC — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A vendor exposes order data only through a paged REST API that returns JSON documents; there are no file drops and no direct database access. The team must land this data daily into a Unity Catalog-governed table. A junior engineer proposes:

```sql
COPY INTO main.ops.orders
FROM 'https://api.vendor.com/v2/orders'
FILEFORMAT = JSON;
```

What is the correct approach?
options: Run the proposed statement with FORMAT_OPTIONS ('header' = 'true') added, so that the HTTP endpoint becomes readable as JSON
Ask the vendor to publish the data to Kafka, because REST API sources cannot be landed in Unity Catalog tables
Register the API URL as a Unity Catalog external location so that COPY INTO treats it as cloud object storage
Write a notebook that pages through the API and appends to a UC-governed table, scheduled as a Lakeflow Job task
snapshot.referenceTitle: Lakeflow Jobs — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A junior engineer tries to start an incremental read of a Kafka topic called orders on a Confluent cluster:

```python
df = (spark.read
  .format("confluent")
  .option("bootstrap", "broker1:9092")
  .option("topic", "orders")
  .load())
```

The call fails immediately. Which correction correctly starts the streaming read so that the JSON message bodies can be parsed into a Delta table?
options: Use spark.readStream.format("kafka") with kafka.bootstrap.servers and subscribe set to "orders"; parse the binary columns downstream
Keep spark.read and just change the format to "kafka"; batch reads automatically become incremental once the result is written to a Delta table
Use spark.readStream.format("cloudFiles") with cloudFiles.format set to "kafka" so that Auto Loader discovers new messages as they arrive
Use spark.readStream.format("jdbc") with the broker URL, because Kafka exposes a JDBC interface for external consumers
snapshot.referenceTitle: Connect to Apache Kafka — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A company is building its lakehouse on the medallion architecture. Several sources feed the first layer: Parquet files in Amazon S3, events from Kafka, and Salesforce data through Lakeflow Connect. Before any transformation is applied, the engineers must agree on what this first layer should contain.

Which statement best describes what belongs in that first layer?
options: Joins and aggregations across all the sources, so that downstream layers only need lightweight filtering to serve consumers
Cleaned, deduplicated, and validated records, so later layers can assume the data is already correct
The raw source data landed as-is and appended incrementally, preserving the original state as the source of truth
Aggregated KPIs for executives, while the raw data stays in an archive bucket outside Unity Catalog
snapshot.referenceTitle: Medallion architecture — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A data engineer is building the silver layer of a medallion pipeline. The bronze table catalog.sales.bronze_customers contains a nullable STRING column named region. For catalog.sales.silver_customers, every customer row must be kept, but region must never be NULL in silver — rows without a region must show the value "Unknown".

```python
bronze = spark.read.table("catalog.sales.bronze_customers")
silver = <cleaning step>
silver.write.saveAsTable("catalog.sales.silver_customers")
```

Which cleaning step meets this requirement?
options: silver = bronze.fillna('Unknown', subset=['region'])
silver = bronze.fillna(0, subset=['region'])
silver = bronze.dropna(subset=['region'])
silver = bronze.withColumn('region', lit('Unknown'))
snapshot.referenceTitle: PySpark function reference — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
The bronze table catalog.crm.bronze_contacts stores two email columns. primary_email is frequently NULL, and some of those rows have a usable secondary_email. The silver view must expose a single column contact_email that returns primary_email when it is not NULL, otherwise secondary_email, and otherwise the literal 'no-email@company.com'.

```sql
SELECT customer_id,
       /* expression here */ AS contact_email
FROM catalog.crm.bronze_contacts
```

Which expression implements this fallback logic?
options: NULLIF(primary_email, secondary_email)
COALESCE('no-email@company.com', primary_email, secondary_email)
COALESCE(primary_email, secondary_email, 'no-email@company.com')
NVL2(primary_email, secondary_email, 'no-email@company.com')
snapshot.referenceTitle: Spark SQL built-in functions — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
An events bronze table landed event_time as STRING values like '2026-03-14 09:30:00' and amount as STRING values like '125.50'. The silver table must standardize the types: event_time as TIMESTAMP and amount as DOUBLE, keeping the same column names and all other columns unchanged.

```python
bronze = spark.read.table("catalog.ops.bronze_events")
silver = <type standardization step>
silver.write.saveAsTable("catalog.ops.silver_events")
```

Which step standardizes the data types correctly?
options: silver = bronze.withColumnRenamed('event_time', 'event_time_ts').withColumnRenamed('amount', 'amount_double').withColumnRenamed('cust', 'customer')
bronze.withColumn('event_time', col('event_time').cast('timestamp')).withColumn('amount', col('amount').cast('double'))
silver = bronze.select(col('event_time').cast('date'), col('amount').cast('double'))
silver = bronze.withColumn('event_time', to_date('event_time'))
snapshot.referenceTitle: PySpark function reference — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
During ingestion design, a junior engineer proposes dropping rows with NULLs and casting every column to its final type before writing to the bronze table, arguing that the silver pipelines would then "just work" with no cleaning code at all. A senior engineer objects, citing the responsibilities of the medallion architecture layers.

Where does this cleaning work belong, and why?
options: In the bronze layer, because bronze must store only validated, strongly typed data before any table is published
In the gold layer, because only gold tables are schema-enforced in Unity Catalog
In the source system, because the medallion architecture requires clean data before any ingestion
In the silver layer — bronze should keep raw data as landed so it can be replayed and audited
snapshot.referenceTitle: Medallion lakehouse architecture — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A silver table of customer contacts is usable as long as a customer can be reached by at least one channel. Rows where BOTH email and phone are NULL must be removed. Rows where only one of the two is NULL must be kept, with the NULL value preserved in place.

```python
bronze = spark.read.table("catalog.crm.bronze_contacts")
silver = <drop rule>
```

Which dropna call implements this rule?
options: silver = bronze.dropna(how='any', subset=['email', 'phone'])
silver = bronze.dropna(how='all', subset=['email', 'phone'])
silver = bronze.dropna(subset=['email'])
silver = bronze.dropna(thresh=2)
snapshot.referenceTitle: PySpark function reference — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:

A PySpark job joins a 4 TB events table with a small dimension table on `user_id`. One stage has 200 tasks: 199 finish in under two minutes, but one task runs for 38 minutes. The stage-level summary metrics show:


options: Too few shuffle partitions: all tasks are uniformly too large, so spark.sql.shuffle.partitions should be increased to shrink every task

A broadcast timeout: the small table exceeded the broadcast threshold and the join fell back to a shuffle

AQE's skew join optimization splits oversized partitions into smaller ones processed in parallel

In Unity Catalog ABAC, what mechanism identifies which columns the policy protects?
options: Governed tags: conditions such as pii = ssn, evaluated with has_tag_value(), match every tagged column — even ones tagged later.
Content inspection: Unity Catalog scans column values at query time and masks anything matching an SSN pattern, with no policy configuration.
Name heuristics: the policy infers sensitive columns from names such as ssn, tax_id, or national_id.
Manual registration: each table owner must list their table's columns in the policy.
snapshot.referenceTitle: Attribute-based access control in Unity Catalog — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A bank runs 200+ Delta tables across the catalogs main and finance. Sensitive columns are classified with governed tags. The governance team must guarantee consistent masking rules for all of them, and — critically — table owners must not be able to weaken or remove the protections on their own tables. New tables are created daily and must be covered automatically once they are tagged.

Which approach meets these requirements?
options: Each table owner writes a masking UDF and runs ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET MASK on their own tables.
ABAC column mask policies at the catalog level using governed tags: automatic coverage, and table owners cannot override them.
The governance team creates one dynamic view per table, embedding is_account_group_member() checks in each view definition.
The governance team grants SELECT on all sensitive tables only to the compliance_team group and tells everyone else to request extracts.
snapshot.referenceTitle: When to use ABAC vs table-level row filters and column masks — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A lead data engineer is preparing a governance review for auditors who want to understand how Databricks protects sensitive data in Unity Catalog. The engineer must accurately compare Unity Catalog ABAC policies with table-level row filters and column masks.

Which statement about the two mechanisms is accurate?
options: ABAC policies replace object-level grants: users matched by a policy can query protected tables without being granted SELECT.
Table-level row filters and column masks are evaluated by Unity Catalog before the query reaches the runtime, while ABAC policies are evaluated inside the query engine afterwards.
ABAC policies attach at catalog or schema level, match via governed tags, and cannot be modified by table owners; table-level masks are owner-managed per table.
Table-level column masks can be attached to many tables at once by tagging the tables, which makes them equivalent to ABAC policies.
snapshot.referenceTitle: When to use ABAC vs table-level row filters and column masks — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A fintech runs its Databricks workspace on classic compute, with all-purpose clusters for interactive notebook work and job clusters for nightly Lakeflow Jobs. During a security review, the cloud architect asks in which cloud account those clusters will run, because that determines network routing and instance policies. Which statement correctly describes how compute is deployed for this workspace?
options: Classic clusters run in the customer's cloud account, in the data plane; the Databricks-managed control plane hosts the UI, job scheduling, and APIs
Every deployment runs all of its compute in Databricks-owned cloud accounts, so customer cloud resources never execute any workloads
The data plane is only a metadata layer for the workspace UI, and all cluster workloads execute inside the Databricks control plane
Serverless compute runs inside the customer's VPC, while classic compute runs in Databricks-owned cloud accounts
snapshot.referenceTitle: Introduction to the Databricks Data Intelligence Platform

snapshot.statement: A data engineer created an all-purpose cluster for interactive notebook work on Friday, used it all day, and then forgot to terminate it before leaving. On Monday, the cloud bill shows the cluster ran — and billed — for the entire weekend, because an administrator had changed the cluster's termination settings at creation. Which default behavior would have stopped the cluster if those settings had been left unchanged?
options: Interactive clusters never terminate on their own by default; termination must be configured and triggered manually
The same default inactivity timeout applies to job clusters, which otherwise stay running between their job runs
All-purpose clusters are created with auto-termination enabled by default, after 120 minutes of inactivity
Auto-termination only affects clusters that use spot instances; on-demand clusters keep running until stopped
snapshot.referenceTitle: Configure clusters — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A data engineering team is standardizing the environment for a long-lived production pipeline. The tech lead asks everyone to select a Databricks Runtime version for the pipeline's clusters, ideally one that will keep receiving fixes for as long as possible. Team members disagree about what the Databricks Runtime actually is and what an LTS version offers. Which statement is correct?
options: Databricks Runtime is only the operating system image installed on the cluster's nodes, with no data processing libraries included
Databricks Runtime packages Apache Spark, Delta Lake, and core libraries, and LTS versions receive fixes for an extended period
Databricks Runtime LTS versions are the oldest and slowest releases available, so new pipelines should always use the latest non-LTS version instead
Databricks Runtime versions are picked automatically for each notebook session, and cannot be pinned on the cluster
snapshot.referenceTitle: Compute — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A new Auto Loader stream must ingest events from a landing directory that already holds two years of history: about one million small JSON files produced by a decommissioned legacy platform. Going forward, only a few dozen new files arrive each day. The stream's very first micro-batch tried to absorb the entire backlog at once and the job ran out of memory. How should the team bound the initial load?
options: Split the source directory into one prefix per year and run one Auto Loader stream per year, all in parallel
Set cloudFiles.maxFilesPerTrigger to a fixed cap, so each micro-batch ingests at most that many files and the backlog drains gradually
Turn cloudFiles.useNotifications off for the first run, because file notification mode is what forces huge micro-batches
Raise the worker count on the job cluster so the single first micro-batch has enough memory to process the whole backlog
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Auto Loader? — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A team starts a new Auto Loader stream on a bucket that already contains three years of legacy extracts from a retired system. Those historical files will be loaded once by a separate backfill script; the stream itself must capture only the files that arrive from its first run onward. How should the stream be configured so the legacy extracts are never ingested?
options: Delete the legacy extracts from the bucket before starting the stream, so the first run finds nothing old to pick up
Use COPY INTO for this table instead, because COPY INTO always skips files that already existed in the folder before its very first execution
Create the target table with a date filter on ingestion time, which Auto Loader honors when it discovers new files
Set cloudFiles.includeExistingFiles to false, so the first run ignores files already in the bucket and ingests only new arrivals
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Auto Loader? — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: An online retailer's operational data lives in a MySQL database: product catalog, inventory, and orders. The analytics platform needs an initial copy of every table in Unity Catalog-governed tables, followed by continuous replication of inserts, updates, and row deletions as they happen, with no ingestion code for the data team to write or operate. Which approach meets these requirements?
options: A Lakeflow Connect database connector: it takes an initial snapshot of each table and then streams ongoing changes, including deletes, into Unity Catalog-governed streaming tables
A scheduled COPY INTO statement that reads the MySQL tables directly and appends their new rows into a Delta table every night
A nightly Lakeflow Job that reads full table snapshots over JDBC and overwrites the target Delta tables with each night's copy
A Lakeflow Connect Kafka connector pointed at the MySQL server, so row changes flow from the database into a streaming table
snapshot.referenceTitle: Lakeflow Connect connector concepts — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A team defines a streaming table in a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline using the read_files table-valued function over a landing directory, and the table's refresh schedule runs every 15 minutes. Files land in that directory around the clock. A new engineer assumes each refresh re-reads the entire directory and worries about duplicate rows. What does each scheduled refresh actually process?
options: Only the files that have arrived since the last successful refresh, because the streaming table keeps durable state tracking what it has already ingested
Every file in the directory, with duplicate rows removed afterwards by a deduplication step that the pipeline runs automatically
Nothing, until an external scheduler updates a control table listing which files the previous refresh already consumed
Only new files if the table was declared with AUTO CDC INTO; streaming tables fed by read_files always reload in full
snapshot.referenceTitle: Streaming tables (Lakeflow pipelines) — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A Lakeflow Job runs an Auto Loader stream on a job cluster and terminates the cluster after each run. The stream's checkpointLocation points at a scratch path on storage that the job wipes and recreates empty whenever a new cluster starts. Every morning, the target Delta table contains duplicate rows re-ingested from the full landing directory. Where is the configuration error?
options: The checkpointLocation points at ephemeral storage; the checkpoint must live in durable cloud storage, in a location dedicated to this stream alone
The checkpointLocation is fine as configured, because the DBFS root of the workspace is the recommended default location for production stream state
The checkpointLocation is irrelevant, because checkpoints are optional when the stream writes its output into a Delta table
The checkpointLocation can be any random path, because Auto Loader rebuilds an equivalent checkpoint from the target table on every run
snapshot.referenceTitle: Auto Loader best practices — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A team's ingestion notebooks currently reference raw files by full s3:// URIs, with long-lived cloud credentials pasted directly into the code. The governance program now requires that every landing location be a centrally governed path, that no cloud credentials appear in notebooks, and that access be granted and revoked through one central permission model. Where should the landing files be stored?
options: In the current bucket as is, with instance profiles referenced inside each notebook and updated by hand whenever the cloud credentials rotate
In the bucket through DBFS mounts configured with cloud credentials on the cluster, the traditional pattern for production landing areas
In a Unity Catalog volume, using /Volumes/catalog/schema/volume paths governed by READ VOLUME and WRITE VOLUME privileges
In a public bucket with anonymous access enabled, so the notebooks can keep using plain s3:// URLs without credential management
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Unity Catalog? — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: One shared landing directory receives deliveries from many producers: clickstream exports, audit logs, invoice images, and order events, all mixed in the same path. Only the files named with the pattern orders-*.csv may ever reach the orders table; everything else must be ignored automatically, with no manual file handling between runs. Which ingestion approach meets this requirement?
options: A COPY INTO statement with a PATTERN clause of orders-*.csv, so only the files whose names match the pattern are loaded
A staging load of every file in the directory, followed by a DELETE that removes the rows originating from non-order files
A manual archive step that moves every non-order file to another prefix before each run, leaving only the matching files in place
An Auto Loader stream with cloudFiles.pathGlobFilter set to orders-*.csv, so only files matching the glob pattern are ingested
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Auto Loader? — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A Lakeflow Job task calls a partner REST API that uses OAuth 2.0 client-credentials authentication: the task presents a client ID and a long-lived client secret to obtain a short-lived access token at runtime. The security team requires that the secret be stored in one managed place, referenced from the task without the value appearing in run history or logs. Where should the client secret be stored?
options: As a string parameter on the Lakeflow Job, so the task reads the secret from its parameter list at the start of every run
In a Databricks secret scope, fetched at runtime with dbutils.secrets.get, which redacts the value in output and logs
In an environment variable set in the cluster's Spark configuration, where it is readable by anyone who can attach to that cluster
In the Git folder repository that holds the pipeline code, with branch permissions restricted to the data engineering team
snapshot.referenceTitle: Manage secrets — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: An operations dashboard queries a Delta table that must never be more than a few minutes out of date. The team runs an Auto Loader stream on always-on compute and wants a new micro-batch to run every 60 seconds, around the clock, without manual intervention. Which trigger configuration produces that behavior?
options: Use .trigger(processingTime='1 minute'): the query schedules continuous micro-batches, each starting about one minute after the previous
Use .trigger(availableNow=True) with a one-minute interval: the stream processes whatever is available and then starts again every minute
Use .trigger(processingTime='1 minute') for discovery only: Auto Loader scans for files faster, while micro-batches follow the default cadence
Use no trigger at all: streams default to batch execution, so the table only advances when someone runs a manual refresh command
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Auto Loader? — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A company runs several Lakeflow Connect managed connectors, and three of them read from PostgreSQL databases that all accept the same service-account credential. The platform team wants to store that credential exactly once, reference it from each connector, and guarantee that engineers who configure or use the connectors can never see the secret value itself. Where do Lakeflow Connect managed connectors hold their source credentials?
options: In a workspace-backed secret scope that every engineer who configures a connector must be granted permission to read
In plaintext variables defined in the team's Automation Bundle and versioned in Git together with the pipeline definitions
In a Unity Catalog connection created with CREATE CONNECTION; connectors reference it and the stored secret stays hidden
In a personal access token issued to each engineer, shared with teammates whenever someone joins or leaves the team
snapshot.referenceTitle: Lakeflow Connect connector concepts — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A streaming table created with read_files over a landing directory has been live for weeks. A faulty transformation in the pipeline polluted its contents; the source files are still intact in cloud storage, and the transformation has now been fixed. The team decides to rebuild the table with a full refresh. Which statement describes what REFRESH TABLE ... FULL REFRESH does?
options: It re-executes only the micro-batches whose output the faulty transformation affected, leaving every correctly loaded batch untouched in the table
It discards the streaming state that tracks processed data and reprocesses everything from the source, fully re-deriving the table
It drops and recreates the table schema before reloading, resetting column types and constraints to their original definitions
It fires automatically whenever the source schema changes, so issuing it manually after fixing a transformation is redundant
snapshot.referenceTitle: Streaming tables (Lakeflow pipelines) — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A scheduled Lakeflow Job runs this statement every night to load the day's files into a reporting table:

```sql
COPY INTO main.ops.deliveries_raw
FROM '/Volumes/main/ops/landing/deliveries/'
FILEFORMAT = CSV;
```

Last night the run failed halfway through, when it hit a corrupted file after several valid files had already been read. What is the state of the target table this morning?
options: Unchanged: COPY INTO is atomic, no partial data was committed, and a rerun after the fix loads all still-pending files
Partially loaded: the valid files read before the corruption were committed, and a rerun resumes from the file after the corrupted one
Empty: the failed statement rolled the table back to its creation state, and the next successful run reloads everything from scratch
Locked: the failed run marked every listed file as loaded, so the team must purge the copy history before it can retry
snapshot.referenceTitle: Get started using COPY INTO — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A company's gold layer ends with a nightly aggregated orders table that a legacy planning system can only consume from its own PostgreSQL database. Right after the aggregation finishes each night, the table's full contents must be delivered into a PostgreSQL table that the legacy system reads. How should the team deliver the gold table into PostgreSQL?
options: Run COPY INTO against the PostgreSQL table, because COPY INTO moves data between Delta tables and any external SQL database
Share the gold table using Delta Sharing: the open protocol automatically materializes it as a table inside the PostgreSQL database
Schedule a notebook that displays the aggregation results and exports them to CSV, letting the legacy team load the file by hand
Add a task that writes the DataFrame with .format('jdbc'), passing the PostgreSQL URL, credentials, and save mode as options
snapshot.referenceTitle: Query databases using JDBC — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
During a performance review of a silver pipeline, a reviewer notices that the author registered a Python UDF to uppercase a country code and to split a full name, although both transformations are available as built-in Spark functions. The author asks why the reviewer insists on replacing the UDF with the native functions.

Which explanation is correct?
options: Built-in functions execute in the optimized engine with no Python serialization and remain visible to the optimizer.
Python UDFs are always faster than built-in functions because they run dedicated code compiled for each transformation.
Built-in functions are exposed only in SQL; PySpark DataFrames must go through a Python UDF for equivalent logic.
Performance is identical for both approaches, so replacing the UDF is purely a matter of coding style preference.
snapshot.referenceTitle: Spark SQL built-in functions — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A PySpark job reads a Delta table into a DataFrame that currently has 200 partitions spread across the cluster. Before writing the result, the team wants to end up with 8 partitions to avoid producing hundreds of tiny output files, but without paying for a full shuffle of the data.

Which operation should they use?
options: repartition(8), the only DataFrame operation able to reduce the number of partitions
coalesce(8), which always preserves the current data distribution across the worker nodes
coalesce(8), which merges existing partitions into fewer ones without a full shuffle
either operation, because repartition and coalesce are synonyms that differ only in naming
snapshot.referenceTitle: PySpark API reference — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A junior engineer chains several DataFrame operations in a notebook: two withColumn calls, a filter on status, and a select of five columns. Each cell returns almost instantly, and she is surprised that the source table is only read minutes later, when she finally calls count(). She asks her lead what happened.

Which explanation is correct?
options: Each transformation executed immediately and stored its result; count() only aggregated the precomputed data.
Transformations are lazy and only extend the logical plan; count() is an action that triggers execution.
Actions are lazy as well; only show() forces Spark to execute the plan and read the source data.
The accumulated plan is executed automatically at cluster shutdown, when pending work is flushed to storage.
snapshot.referenceTitle: PySpark API reference — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
Two analysts on different teams must share the same SQL definition — a curated customer list built over several silver tables. The definition must live in one governed place: secured with Unity Catalog permissions, centrally versioned, and readable from any workspace attached to the metastore. The analysts use separate notebooks on separate compute.

Which object meets these requirements?
options: A temporary view (CREATE TEMP VIEW), which lives only inside the session that defines it
A global temporary view (CREATE GLOBAL TEMP VIEW), shared across sessions on the same cluster
A .sql script in a shared folder, which each analyst must open and run in her own session
A view created with CREATE VIEW in a Unity Catalog schema, stored in the metastore and governed with grants
snapshot.referenceTitle: CREATE VIEW — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
Last night, a batch job ran a faulty UPDATE on catalog.sales.orders, overwriting the status column on every row. The faulty commit landed as version 3, and the table is now at version 4. An analyst must produce a report from the table exactly as it existed before that commit, without changing the current data.

How should the analyst read the pre-UPDATE snapshot?
options: Query the historical snapshot with SELECT * FROM catalog.sales.orders VERSION AS OF 2
Run RESTORE TABLE catalog.sales.orders TO VERSION AS OF 2, then execute the report again
Run the report on the current table with a WHERE clause that filters out the overwritten rows
Read the table's underlying Parquet data files directly from the storage location with Spark
snapshot.referenceTitle: Delta Lake guide — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
An auditor must verify catalog.finance.ledger as it stood 20 days ago. The team runs the time travel query for that snapshot, but it fails with a FILE_NOT_FOUND exception pointing at a data file. The table is vacuumed weekly with the default retention settings, and OPTIMIZE also runs regularly.

What is the most likely cause of the failure?
options: Time travel preserves every version since table creation, so the failure must come from missing SELECT privileges
VACUUM only compacts small files into larger ones and never deletes any file from storage
VACUUM removed data files older than the default 7-day retention, making older snapshots unreadable
RESTORE TABLE can recover any prior version even after VACUUM has removed the underlying files
snapshot.referenceTitle: Best practices: Delta Lake — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A streaming pipeline commits new data to catalog.ops.events every 30 seconds. After a few months, the Delta table holds hundreds of thousands of small files, and dashboard queries have degraded: execution time is dominated by listing and opening files rather than scanning data.

Which maintenance action restores read performance?
options: Run VACUUM with the default retention settings, so that small files are merged into larger ones
Run OPTIMIZE, which compacts the small files into larger ones for more efficient reads
Rewrite the entire table every night with repartition(1) to produce one giant file
Scale up the compute behind the dashboards while leaving the file layout untouched
snapshot.referenceTitle: Best practices: Delta Lake — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
Every dashboard query against catalog.sales.orders derives the order date by calling to_date(order_ts) — an expression repeated across dozens of reports over billions of rows. The team wants the derived value computed once, at write time, and physically stored as a column of the table.

Which Delta Lake feature provides this?
options: A view that computes to_date(order_ts) on every read of the underlying table
A trigger that fires AFTER INSERT on the table and updates the derived column
A dashboard-level expression, so that the calculation stays out of the storage layer
A generated column: order_date DATE GENERATED ALWAYS AS (CAST(order_ts AS DATE))
snapshot.referenceTitle: Delta Lake guide — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
An operational database streams its change feed into a bronze table: each row carries the operation (insert, update, delete), a monotonically increasing sequence number, and the changed columns. In a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline, the team must keep a streaming table in sync with the current source state — deletes included — without writing manual merge logic.

Which construct should the pipeline declare?
options: A hand-written MERGE INTO statement that joins the change rows to the target on the primary key
An AUTO CDC INTO flow with KEYS and SEQUENCE BY, replacing the former APPLY CHANGES syntax
A row-level expectation that drops invalid change rows as they flow into the target table
A full refresh that recreates the streaming table from scratch whenever a new batch arrives
snapshot.referenceTitle: The AUTO CDC APIs (Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines) — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A Delta table catalog.sales.payments declares amount as DOUBLE. A new ingestion job builds a DataFrame in which amount is still STRING, with raw values like '125.50', and appends the DataFrame to the table. The job author asks what Delta Lake will do when the write is attempted.

What is the expected behavior?
options: The write fails: Delta enforces the table schema and rejects a column type that does not match
The write succeeds, storing STRING values that are converted back to DOUBLE whenever readers query
Delta automatically adds a second column, amount_string, to hold the mismatched incoming values
Delta writes only the columns whose types are compatible and silently drops the mismatched one
snapshot.referenceTitle: Delta Lake guide — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
Before promoting a new PySpark transformation into the nightly production job, an engineer wants to see what Spark intends to do with it — the planned join strategy, the filters, and the projection — without spending cluster resources actually running the query.

Which action gives her this preview?
options: Call count() after every transformation and compare the elapsed time of each stage
Nothing — lazy evaluation makes the plan unknowable until the query has fully executed
Call df.explain() to print the logical and physical plans without executing anything
Run the job in production and inspect the Spark UI, the only place where plans appear
snapshot.referenceTitle: PySpark API reference — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A reconciliation job must align catalog.sales.silver_orders with the source extract catalog.sales.latest_orders in one atomic pass: matched orders get their status refreshed, matched orders whose source status is 'CANCELLED' must be removed from the target, and unmatched source orders must be inserted.

```sql
MERGE INTO catalog.sales.silver_orders AS t
USING catalog.sales.latest_orders AS s
ON t.order_id = s.order_id
-- WHEN clauses omitted
```

Which approach meets all three requirements in this single atomic pass?
options: Run two MERGE statements in sequence: one that updates matched rows and inserts new ones, then one that deletes the cancelled orders
Use a single MERGE with WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET * and WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *, issuing a separate DELETE for the cancelled orders
Use a single MERGE with WHEN MATCHED AND s.status = 'CANCELLED' THEN DELETE, then WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *, then WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *
Replace the MERGE with an UPDATE on the matched rows followed by REPLACE WHERE, rewriting the table with the surviving and new orders
snapshot.referenceTitle: Merge data (Delta Lake upsert) — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
Over the past week, catalog.ops.shipments has behaved strangely: row counts shift overnight even though the team's own jobs were idle, and the table version keeps climbing. The engineer needs to determine exactly which operations were committed to the table, when, and by which user or service principal.

Which command gives her this commit-level audit trail?
options: SHOW TABLES with a filter on the last modified date, which lists only recent writes
A manual read of the _delta_log JSON transaction log files parsed directly from storage
The workspace audit log, which is described as the only existing record of table writes
DESCRIBE HISTORY, which lists every commit with its operation, timestamp, and user
snapshot.referenceTitle: Delta Lake guide — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
The source system exports two timestamps as STRING columns: ordered_at and shipped_at, both formatted like '2026-07-02 14:45:00'. In the silver transformation, the team must add fulfillment_days with the number of calendar days between the order date and the ship date, written in Spark SQL.

Which approach should they use?
options: Parse both columns with to_timestamp(col, 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss'), then compute datediff(shipped_at, ordered_at)
Slice fixed character positions with substring() to build year, month, and day, then subtract the dates
Convert both columns with unix_timestamp(), subtract, and divide the difference by 86400
Register a Python UDF, because date parsing requires a library that Spark SQL lacks natively
snapshot.referenceTitle: Spark SQL built-in functions — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
The table catalog.sales.order_items stores one row per line item, with columns order_id and item. An export job must return exactly one row per order, carrying all of its items in a single ARRAY<STRING> column named items — a native array, not a concatenated string.

Which query shape produces this result?
options: Explode the item column first, then concatenate the values into one delimited string
SELECT order_id, collect_list(item) AS items FROM catalog.sales.order_items GROUP BY order_id
Pivot the rows into one explicit column per item position, such as item_1 and item_2
It is impossible in pure SQL, because aggregate functions cannot return complex types like arrays
snapshot.referenceTitle: Spark SQL built-in functions — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A production Lakeflow Job that publishes Unity Catalog tables was created by a senior data engineer who left the company last month. His user account has since been removed, and the job's nightly runs now fail with permission errors when reading the source tables. The job's code and schedule are correct.

What should the team change to make the job independent of any person's account?
options: Set the job's Run as identity to a production service principal that holds the required table grants
Set Run as to the new team lead now, and to whoever leads the team after each reorganization
Leave Run as empty, since production jobs automatically run with the permissions of whoever triggered them
Grant the departed engineer's user account the workspace admin role so that its permissions are never removed again
snapshot.referenceTitle: Manage permissions on Lakeflow Jobs — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A team maintains a shared Python module, data_prep.py, which lives in the team's Git repository and is reviewed through pull requests. Several production pipelines depend on it. They are adding a task to a Lakeflow Job that must execute this file exactly as it exists on the main branch, with no manual copies.

How should the task be configured?
options: Paste the module's current code into a notebook task and refresh that copy by hand whenever the module changes
Copy data_prep.py into the workspace first, because Lakeflow Jobs can only execute notebook tasks
Use a Python script task with the Git provider as its source, pointing to data_prep.py on the main branch
Run the script manually in a terminal on an attached cluster and load the exported CSV files afterward
snapshot.referenceTitle: Configure and edit tasks in Lakeflow Jobs — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A data engineering team must run a Lakeflow Job at 02:00 every weekday, Monday through Friday, so that reporting tables are fresh before analysts arrive. In the job's schedule settings, they open the cron expression editor to type the schedule by hand.

Which expression should they enter?
options: 0 2 * * MON-FRI
MON-FRI 02:00
0 0 2 ? * MON-FRI *
snapshot.referenceTitle: Configure and edit Lakeflow Jobs — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A task in a production Lakeflow Job got stuck in an infinite loop over the weekend. Nobody was watching, and the job stayed in the running state for three days, holding compute and blocking downstream pipelines. The team wants a stuck run like this to be stopped and marked as failed automatically.

What should they configure?
options: Nothing — Lakeflow Jobs offer no timeout setting, so a stuck run must be detected and canceled manually
The job cluster's auto-termination setting, which terminates compute that has been idle for the configured minutes
A timeout on scheduled runs only, because runs started manually with Run now are allowed to run indefinitely
A Timeout setting on the job or the task, so that exceeding the limit stops the run with a Timed Out status
snapshot.referenceTitle: Configure and edit Lakeflow Jobs — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
When a nightly Lakeflow Job fails, the team already receives an email notification. Operations, however, also needs every failure recorded in its own incident system, which exposes an HTTP endpoint, and the on-call rotation must be paged through PagerDuty. All of this should happen automatically as part of the run.

How can the team meet this requirement?
options: Keep email as the notification, since Databricks cannot target external systems, and let the incident system poll the jobs API
Add a webhook destination to the job's failure notification, so that Databricks posts a JSON payload to the endpoint
Add a final task that calls the incident system's endpoint itself at the end of every run
Switch the job to a file arrival trigger, because webhook notifications only work for event-triggered jobs
snapshot.referenceTitle: Add notifications on a job — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
The production version of an ETL notebook lives on the release branch of the team's GitHub repository. Today, a team member copies the notebook into the workspace by hand before each release, and last week's job ran a stale copy that missed two reviewed fixes. The next release must run exactly the reviewed code, with no manual steps.

How should the notebook task be configured?
options: Keep the manual copy, but add a release checklist that verifies the workspace version before each run
Leave the task pointing at the workspace, because jobs can only execute notebooks stored there
Set the task's Source to the Git provider and point it at the notebook on the release branch
Point the task at a /Repos workspace path and trust each developer to pull the release branch before the run
snapshot.referenceTitle: Notebook task for jobs — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A Lakeflow Job runs ingest, transform, and publish as a linear chain. The team must add an alerting task that runs only when the ingest task fails — it must never run when the pipeline succeeds. The alerting code is ready; only the task's wiring is missing.

How should the alerting task be wired into the job?
options: Depends on ingest with the Run if condition All failed, so it runs only when ingest has failed
No dependencies — it runs in every run, queries the previous run's outcome through the API, and exits early on success
Depends on publish with the default Run if condition, closing the chain after every successful run
A second, identical job that contains only the alerting task and is triggered by hand when the first job fails

snapshot.statement:
A daily Lakeflow Job must fire at 06:00 in the company's Sao Paulo office (America/Sao_Paulo). The platform team in Paris created the schedule, so its timezone is Europe/Paris and its cron fires at 11:00 — 06:00 in Sao Paulo during the European summer. In late October, Europe ended daylight saving time, and the job began firing at 07:00 local.

How does the team make the firing time deterministic?
options: Set the schedule's timezone to America/Sao_Paulo, so the cron is always resolved in Sao Paulo time
Keep Europe/Paris and edit the cron hour by hand twice a year, when European clocks change
Set spark.sql.session.timeZone to America/Sao_Paulo in the job's tasks, so the scheduler fires in local time
Leave the timezone alone, because a job's cron automatically follows the local timezone of the engineer who created it
snapshot.referenceTitle: Configure and edit Lakeflow Jobs — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A Lakeflow Job orchestrates an end-to-end flow: a notebook task lands raw files, then a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline must process the new data, and a final task exports the curated tables. The team is now adding the middle step to the job.

How does the pipeline take part in this job?
options: As a Pipeline task, which always triggers a full refresh of the pipeline before processing
It cannot, because pipelines run only as standalone objects with their own schedules
As a notebook task that re-runs the pipeline's source notebook inside the job
As a Pipeline task that selects the pipeline and triggers a refresh — incremental by default

snapshot.statement:
A nightly Lakeflow Job takes a processing_date parameter whose default is the current date. Late this evening, an on-call engineer must reprocess yesterday's data exactly once, and tomorrow's scheduled run must continue using the default. The job definition itself may not change.

What should the engineer do?
options: Edit the job's default parameter to yesterday's date, start the run, and revert the default before the nightly schedule fires
Clone the job into a one-off reprocess version with the new date, run it, and delete the clone afterwards
Start the run with Run now with different parameters, passing processing_date for that run only
Deploy a new bundle target that sets the parameter, since parameter values can only change through a deployment

snapshot.statement:
A Lakeflow Job's transformations require pandas 2.x. The team has been prototyping on a shared cluster that other teams also depend on, and that cluster has pandas 1.5 pinned — upgrading it would break the other teams' workloads. The job is about to go to production.

Where should pandas 2.x be installed for this job?
options: On the shared cluster, after warning the other teams and having them retest their pipelines
With %pip install at the top of the job's notebook, which fixes the version for every job the same way
Nowhere, because pinned libraries are not supported on job clusters, so the code must avoid pandas 2.x
On the job's own job cluster, whose library list is isolated from the compute other teams share

snapshot.statement: A newly hired data engineer wants to start adopting Automation Bundles for the team's Lakeflow Jobs and pipelines. They need a first bundle project on their laptop — a databricks.yml plus starter resource definitions — but have never written bundle YAML and do not want to assemble the project files by hand. Which action gets them a working scaffold the fastest?
options: Copy a full databricks.yml example out of the Databricks documentation and adapt its fields by hand each time the team starts a new project
Ask a workspace administrator to create the bundle in the workspace UI, because bundles cannot be created locally
Connect a remote Git repository to the workspace first, because databricks bundle init will not run without an existing repository
Run databricks bundle init, pick one of the Databricks-provided default templates, and answer the prompts that generate the project files

snapshot.statement: A team's CI pipeline deploys every open pull request as its own Automation Bundle target — pr_142, pr_143, and so on — creating a disposable copy of the pipeline's Lakeflow Job and notebooks in a shared dev workspace. Pull request 142 has just been merged, and the pipeline must clean up that PR's deployment completely, leaving no orphaned jobs, notebooks, or artifacts, without touching other pull requests' resources. What should the merge step run?
options: Delete the shared dev workspace after every merge and let the next pull request deployment recreate everything inside it
Run nothing in the merge step — the PR deployment's job cluster auto-terminates after its runs, removing the deployed resources with it
Run databricks bundle destroy and accept its side effect of permanently deleting the bundle's source files and Git repository
Run databricks bundle destroy -t pr_142, which deletes the job, files, and artifacts that this target's deployment created

snapshot.statement: A team deploys one Automation Bundle to dev and prod targets. In dev only, the group data_team must hold CAN_MANAGE_RUN on the bundle's Lakeflow Job so members can trigger and monitor runs; in prod the group must receive nothing. The team wants the grant applied automatically on every deploy and reviewed in Git like the rest of the configuration. How should this be set up?
options: Add a permissions entry granting data_team the CAN_MANAGE_RUN level on the job resource within the dev target of the bundle
Have an administrator grant CAN_MANAGE_RUN to data_team from the job's Permissions tab in the dev workspace UI after every deploy
Make data_team a workspace admin in the dev workspace so its members can run every job there without bundle changes
Skip permissions in the bundle, because bundle permissions mappings can only grant view-level access such as CAN_VIEW

snapshot.statement: A team's Automation Bundle has grown into a single 600-line databricks.yml: two Lakeflow Jobs, one pipeline, and per-environment overrides for dev, test, and prod all live in one file that reviewers struggle to read. The engineers want resource definitions in their own files, with each target spelling out only what differs from the root definitions. How should the bundle be restructured?
options: Keep everything in one databricks.yml, because the bundle specification recommends keeping all resource definitions and targets together in a single configuration file
Move the job and pipeline definitions into resource files listed in the include mapping; targets inherit root definitions and override only what changes
Create a separate bundle per environment, duplicating the job and pipeline definitions in each one to keep the files short
Give up on splitting the file: a bundle cannot reference other files, so the single databricks.yml must simply be reorganized internally

snapshot.statement: A nightly GitHub Actions workflow authenticates as the service principal ci-deployer and runs databricks bundle deploy -t prod, creating and updating the team's Lakeflow Jobs and pipelines in the production workspace. Security policy requires machine identities to hold the narrowest access that still lets the pipeline deploy successfully. Which privilege assignment satisfies the policy?
options: Make ci-deployer an account admin, so the nightly deploy can never fail because of a missing permission
Rely on inheritance: a service principal automatically holds the permissions of the engineer who authored the bundle
Grant ci-deployer only what the deployment needs: privileges to create and manage its jobs and pipelines, plus required catalog and schema access
Assign no privileges at all, because bundle deployments run under the workspace identity rather than the signed-in principal
